notes.meaning: This opening line gives the title and author of the book. Calling it the Song of Songs is a Hebrew way of saying it is the best and most wonderful song of all. King Solomon wrote it, and traditional readers have seen it as a picture of the great love between Christ and his people.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Many modern scholars see the book primarily as human love poetry celebrating marital love, rather than an allegory of Christ and the church.

notes.meaning: A young woman speaks, longing for close affection and kisses from the one she loves. She declares that his love is sweeter and brings more joy than fine wine. In Christian teaching, this expresses the soul's deep desire for Christ's personal favor and the peace of his promises.

The bride delights in the pleasing scent of her beloved and compares his good name to poured-out perfume. Because his character is so pure and attractive, other young women rightly admire him. For believers, this points to the wonderful grace and name of Jesus, which draw faithful hearts to him.

The young woman asks her lover to lead her away quickly, and she rejoices that the king has brought her into his private rooms. The change from 'me' to 'we' shows that she and her companions share in this gladness. This reminds Christians that we need God's Spirit to draw us to Christ, and believers run to follow him together.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: A popular dramatic interpretation suggests three characters, where a rustic maiden wants to flee from King Solomon's palace to be reunited with her true shepherd lover.

notes.meaning: The woman speaks to the city women of Jerusalem, explaining that her skin has been darkened by working outdoors. Even though she feels dark like the black goatskin tents of desert nomads, she knows she is lovely like the rich curtains of the royal palace. Spiritually, believers often feel weak and spotted in themselves, yet completely beautiful and accepted in Christ.

She tells the women not to look down on her, because her dark skin came from working long hours under the hot sun. Her brothers were harsh with her and forced her to look after their vineyards, leaving her no time to take care of her own appearance. Believers see in this a warning not to let outside burdens or human troubles keep us from tending our own walk with God.

The woman asks her beloved where he grazes his sheep and where he lets them rest during the hottest part of the day. She does not want to wander around veiled and confused among the flocks of other shepherds. In the same way, the Christian soul asks Jesus where he feeds his people so it does not stray into error or spiritual danger.

The shepherd lovingly replies, calling her the most beautiful among women. He tells her that if she does not know where to go, she should simply follow the worn tracks of the sheep and feed her young goats near the shepherds' tents. This teaches believers to follow the faithful footsteps of earlier saints and stay close to God's regular gatherings.

The king compares his bride to a prized mare among Pharaoh's chariot horses. In the ancient world, Egyptian horses were famous for their great strength, swiftness, and beauty. For believers, this shows the high honor and noble strength that Christ gives to his church.

The lover praises her face, which is framed by beautiful ornaments, and her neck, which is dressed in chains of jewels. He promises to give her even richer gifts of gold studded with silver beads. This illustrates how the Lord delights in the spiritual graces he gives his people and promises to add even more beauty to their lives.

The woman tells how the sweet scent of her perfume spread while the king sat at his banquet table. Sitting together at a feast represents close, joyful fellowship between lovers. In spiritual life, this pictures the joyful presence of Christ that brings out thankful praise and love in the hearts of his people.

She compares her beloved to a small pouch of fragrant myrrh resting close against her chest all night. Myrrh was a rare and precious perfume that brought constant sweetness. This paints a warm picture of keeping Christ near to our hearts through faith at all times.

The woman also compares her lover to a cluster of sweet-smelling henna flowers found in the lush oasis of En-gedi. En-gedi was a fertile, green spot filled with life in the middle of a dry wilderness. To the believer, Christ brings refreshing joy and beauty even in the hardest seasons of life.

The man speaks tenderly to the woman, twice telling her that she is beautiful. He says her eyes are like doves, which suggests a gentle, loving, and faithful look. This shows how Christ sees and values purity, gentleness, and sincere love in those who belong to him.

The woman answers back with equal praise, declaring that her beloved is truly handsome and delightful. She describes the green outdoor grass as their resting place, with tall cedar and fir trees serving as the beams and roof of their home. Together, they celebrate the simple, lasting joy of their union under the canopy of God's creation.
